summary: Northern Morocco was under Umayyad governors only from c. 708 until the Berber Revolt of 740, after which it broke away from the caliphate. The 10th century saw the Fatimids and the Umayyads of Córdoba fight over it through local proxies, and Córdoba ruled some coastal towns directly. Real caliphal rule over almost all of Morocco came through the Almoravids (who recognised the Abbasids, c. 1050s–1147) and then the Almohads, a counted caliphate (1147–1269). Later dynasties (Marinids, Wattasids, Saadians, Alaouites) did not recognise an outside caliph. The one exception is Abd al-Malik (1576–78), who had the khutba read in the Ottoman sultan's name.

units.label: Northern Morocco, Fez and Tafilalt (al-Maghrib al-Aqṣā; Sijilmāsa)

caliphate.who: Umayyad governors (Tangier) until the Berber Revolt. In the 10th century, Fatimid and Córdoban-Umayyad direct posts and proxies. Then the Almoravids (recognised the Abbasids) and the Almohad caliphate directly.
caliphate.dates: c. 708–740 Umayyad direct (Tangier); 909 and 958–60 Fatimid campaigns (Sijilmasa, Fez); Córdoba direct at Melilla 927, Ceuta 931, Tangier 951, and Fez via the Maghrawa from 987/88; Almoravid c. 1055 (Sijilmasa) to early 1080s (Fez) until 1147; Almohad 1147–1269

units.notes: Umayyad rule here was short: Musa ibn Nusayr took Tangier c. 705–708, and the Berber Revolt of 740 permanently ended Umayyad control. Under the Idrisids the land was ruled by Muslims but by no caliph. Fatimid and Córdoban control in the 10th century was patchy and contested; Córdoba directly held coastal towns (Melilla, Ceuta, Tangier). The Midrarids of Sijilmasa are listed as nominal Abbasid and then Fatimid vassals. The firm caliphal period is Almoravid (Abbasid-recognising) and Almohad rule.
units.uncertain: Ceuta and Melilla are not in these admin-1 polygons; I used them only as evidence for Córdoba's footing on this coast. The exact length of direct Córdoban rule in Fez (via al-Mansur's governors) was not confirmed in an opened page. The 'nominal vassal' status of the Midrarids comes from the Wikipedia infobox, not checked further.

caliphate.dates: Almoravid conquest c. 1058–1060 to 1147; Almohad 1147–1269 (Barghawata finally eliminated 1149)

units.notes: For about three centuries the Tamesna coast between Salé and Safi was ruled by the Barghawata, whose heterodox religion mixed Islamic and local Berber elements. They recognised no caliph and resisted Córdoba, the Fatimids and the Almoravids; Ibn Yasin was killed fighting them in 1058/59. Caliphal rule begins only with the Almoravid conquest and is completed by the Almohads.
units.uncertain: I could not confirm whether the Umayyad governors (708–740) ever actually administered Tamesna, so I have not claimed it. The Barghawata's exact borders (Bou Regreg to the Oum Er-Rbia, or to Safi) are only approximate.

units.notes: This was the political centre of two caliphal regimes: Almoravid Marrakesh, under Abbasid recognition, and the Almohad caliphate, which arose in the High Atlas (Ibn Tumart proclaimed Mahdi 1121) and ruled from Marrakesh until 1269. Before the Almoravids, I found no verified evidence of caliphal administration here.
units.uncertain: Early Umayyad expeditions (Uqba, Musa) probably crossed this region, but I could not confirm that Umayyad governors were based here.

units.label: Sous and the Draa valley (al-Sūs)

caliphate.who: First, Umayyad expeditions (Uqba, Musa). Then the Almoravids (recognised the Abbasids) and the Almohad caliphate directly.
caliphate.dates: Uqba reached the Atlantic near Agadir 682–683 (raid); Musa ibn Nusayr pushed into the Sus c. 705–708; Almoravid from the 1050s to 1147; Almohad 1147–1269

units.notes: Umayyad armies reached the Sous (Uqba's 682–83 march, Musa's campaign), but these were expeditions rather than lasting administration, and all of it ended in 740. Lasting caliphal rule came with the Almoravids and Almohads. The Saadian dynasty rose here; under Abd al-Malik (1576–78) it briefly had the khutba read for the Ottoman sultan.
units.uncertain: Modern scholars quoted on the conquest page doubt parts of Uqba's march. I did not confirm whether Umayyad governors sat permanently in the Sous before 740.

units.label: Wadi Nun and the northern Saguia el-Hamra (Nūl Lamṭa)

caliphate.who: Almoravids (recognised the Abbasids), possibly the Almohads
caliphate.dates: probably 1050s–1147 (Almoravid); not confirmed

islamic_states.name: Alaouite sultans (allegiance of Ma'qil/Tekna tribes)
islamic_states.dates: 1678 (Moulay Ismail) to 1767; later spiritual allegiance only

units.notes: The Wadi Nun lay on the Almoravid corridor between the Sahara and the Sous, so it was very probably inside the Almoravid realm. I could not open a page that confirms this. In the early modern period the Ma'qil and Tekna tribes of the Wadi Nun gave allegiance to Moulay Ismail (1678), but by 1767 Morocco's treaty with Spain admitted it did not control the Tekna. The Es-Semara part of this province is really Western Saharan Saguia el-Hamra; Smara was only founded in 1869 and was Ma al-Aynayn's religious capital from 1902.
units.uncertain: I could not open the Nul Lamta articles (English or French), so Almoravid and Almohad control of the Wadi Nun is inferred, not checked. If that rule is rejected, this unit drops to islamic_state_ruled. The southern (Smara) part of the polygon has a different, Western Saharan history.

units.label: Western Sahara inside Morocco's admin-1 (Sāqiyat al-Ḥamrāʾ and Wādī al-Dhahab / Río de Oro)

caliphate.who: No verified caliphal administration. This is the Sanhaja homeland of the Almoravid movement, but the Almoravids' Abbasid recognition dates to Yusuf ibn Tashfin's northern state.

islamic_states.name: Moroccan sultans (allegiance of some tribes only)

units.notes: The Almoravid movement grew from the Sanhaja tribes of this desert. Their rule there was a tribal confederation, not an administration with governors. Later, Hassaniya-speaking tribes sometimes gave allegiance (bay'a) to Moroccan sultans. In 1975 the ICJ found ties of allegiance with only some tribes, and no Moroccan or Mauritanian territorial sovereignty. This is a strictly historical classification, not a statement on today's sovereignty dispute.
units.uncertain: It is unclear whether the Saharan Almoravids under Abu Bakr ibn Umar (to 1087) used the Abbasid name; the opened pages tie Abbasid recognition to Yusuf ibn Tashfin. Rating this as an 'Islamic state ruled' land is generous: in practice it may be closer to tribal autonomy with occasional allegiance.

The ICJ (1975) found ties of allegiance with only some tribes, and no territorial sovereignty by Morocco or the Mauritanian entity.

summary: The east (Constantinois, Zab) belonged to Ifriqiya. It was ruled by Umayyad and then Abbasid governors, by the Aghlabids for the Abbasids, and from 909 by the Fatimids, whose movement started among the Kutama of Petite Kabylie. The west and centre were lost to the caliphate in 740 and went to the Rustamid Ibadi imamate and the Idrisids. They came back under caliph-linked rule through the Fatimids and Zirids/Hammadids, the Almoravids and the Almohads. From the 16th century the Ottoman Regency of Algiers (from 1516/1519 to 1830) administered the Tell. The Saharan oases were only tributary or autonomous, and the far south (Ahaggar, Tindouf) was never really ruled.

units.label: Constantinois and Petite Kabylie (western Ifrīqiyah; Kutāma country)

caliphate.who: Umayyad then Abbasid governors. Then the Aghlabids for the Abbasids, the Fatimids directly, the Zirids for the Fatimids, and the Hammadids (alternating Abbasid/Fatimid recognition). Then the Almohad caliphate, and the Ottoman Beylik of Constantine.
caliphate.dates: c. 700s Umayyad (central Numidia/Constantine held by 708); 800–909 Aghlabid; 909–973 Fatimid direct; 973–1015 Zirid; 1015–1152 Hammadid (Béjaïa capital c. 1090–1152); 1152–1229 Almohad; Ottoman Beylik of Constantine 1528–1837

units.notes: This is the most solidly caliph-ruled part of Algeria. Aghlabid towns included Mila and Setif. The Fatimid da'wa began among the Kutama near Ikjan (893). Béjaïa was the Hammadid capital. In the Ottoman era the Beylik of Constantine was the Regency's most populous province, under a bey appointed by the dey.
units.uncertain: Some mountain districts (e.g. Babors, parts of Petite Kabylie) were probably only loosely controlled in every period; I did not check this district by district.

units.label: Aurès, Zab and Hodna (al-Zāb; Ṭubna, al-Masīla)

caliphate.who: Umayyad and Abbasid governors at Tobna (capital of the Zab), Aghlabids for the Abbasids, the Fatimids (founded M'Sila 927), Zirids/Hammadids (Qal'at Bani Hammad in M'Sila), Almohads, the Ottoman Beylik of Constantine
caliphate.dates: c. 700–c. 900 Tobna as Zab capital (Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab governor there before 800); 800–909 Aghlabid; 909–973 Fatimid; 1015–1152 Hammadid; 1152–1229 Almohad; 1528–1830s Ottoman beylik

units.notes: Tobna (Batna province) was the governors' capital of the Zab for about two centuries, so the lowlands were firmly administered. The Aurès mountains were the base of the Kahina's resistance (defeated c. 701) and later of Ibadi Hawwara rebels against the Fatimids (947), so the high Aurès were probably more loosely held. Biskra had a Hammadid governor and later belonged to the Ottoman Beylik of Constantine.
units.uncertain: How far each regime controlled the interior Aurès massif, as opposed to the Zab and Hodna plains, was not checked.

caliphate.who: Zirids (for the Fatimids) and Hammadids (Algiers governed by a Hammadid prince), Almoravids (Abbasid recognition), the Almohad caliphate, then the Ottoman Regency of Algiers (Beylik of Titteri at Médéa)

units.notes: Umayyad control of this area before 740 is not documented in the pages I opened. From the late 10th century the area was held by caliph-recognising dynasties. Algiers was the Ottoman Regency's capital, with the sultan named in the khutba and on coins even after the deys became practically independent (1659–1830).
units.uncertain: I did not verify Zirid rule over Algiers, Médéa and Miliana in an opened page; the Hammadid page confirms a Hammadid governor in Algiers.

units.label: Greater Kabylia (land of the Zwāwa; Kingdom of Kuku)

caliphate.who: The Ottoman Regency of Algiers held forts (bordjs) in the Sebaou and neighbouring valleys. Before that, Hammadid/Almohad reach into the mountains is unclear.
caliphate.dates: Ottoman forts 18th c. (Tazarart 1710s, Boghni 1724); Kuku a tributary 'feudatory' of Algiers from the mid-16th c.

units.notes: The high Kabyle mountains largely governed themselves. The Kingdom of Kuku allied with, fought and later paid modest tribute and troops to Ottoman Algiers. Ottoman garrisons and forts held only the valleys and were repeatedly destroyed. The caliphal rating rests on the valleys; the mountains were closer to tributary.
units.uncertain: I found no verified evidence on how far the Hammadids (based nearby at Béjaïa) or the Almohads controlled Greater Kabylia. Splitting valley from mountain is not possible at province level.

units.label: Western Tell / Oranie (Tilimsān)

caliphate.who: Umayyad conquest (708) until 740. Then the Maghrawa of Ziri ibn Atiyya under Córdoban Umayyad protection, the Almoravids (Abbasid recognition), the Almohad caliphate directly, and the Ottoman Regency (Beylik of the West).

units.notes: After the Arab conquest (708), the region left caliphal control in 740 and was ruled by Idrisid and Zenata Muslim powers. Caliph-linked rule came through Córdoba's Zenata clients, the Almoravids and the Almohads. The Zayyanids recognised no caliph. Ottoman rule began at Tlemcen in 1551, but Oran stayed Spanish until 1792.
units.uncertain: I did not open an Ottoman–Spanish timeline for Oran (including any interval of Ottoman rule before 1792). Whether the Zayyanids gave any formal recognition to the Hafsid caliphal claim was not established.

caliphate.who: Recognised nominal Ottoman authority (Regency of Algiers) while keeping internal autonomy

units.notes: The Mzab towns were founded by Ibadi refugees after the Rustamid fall and governed themselves under their own religious councils. They accepted Ottoman suzerainty only nominally, then paid France a contribution from 1853 until annexation in 1882.
units.uncertain: Whether the Mzab paid a regular tribute to Algiers or only had a negotiated autonomy is unclear: the Ghardaïa university abstract describes autonomy with loyalty rather than tribute.

From 1552 the Banu Djellab of Touggourt and the Ouargla rulers were Ottoman vassals who paid tribute but governed themselves. In practice this was mostly local Muslim rule with brief or nominal caliphal overlordship.
units.uncertain: How long the Hammadid governorship lasted is unknown. If it was brief, the honest category is islamic_state_ruled or tributary. The Souf's (El Oued's) own relation to Touggourt or Constantine was not checked. Pre-2019 Ouargla province also covered Touggourt; I treated it that way.

units.notes: The Kel Ahaggar Tuareg confederation, descended in part from the Ibadi Hawwara who fled the Aurès after 947, governed itself until French suzerainty in 1902–1903. Islam spread here through these migrations and the caravan trade, not through any state's rule.

summary: Tunisia was the heart of Ifriqiya and the most continuously caliph-ruled land in the Maghreb. Its rulers in turn were Umayyad governors from Kairouan (670), the Aghlabids for the Abbasids (800–909), the Fatimids directly (909–973) and the Zirids for the Fatimids. The Zirids switched to the Abbasids around 1048. After that came the Almohads (1159–1229) and the Ottomans (1574–1881). The Hafsids (1229–1574) recognised no outside caliph and claimed the caliphate themselves from 1253.

units.label: Northern and central Tunisia (core of Ifrīqiyah: Qayrawān, Tūnis, al-Mahdiyya)

caliphate.who: First a Rashidun raid (Sufetula 647). Then Umayyad and Abbasid governors at Kairouan, the Aghlabids for the Abbasids, the Fatimid caliphs (capital Mahdia), and the Zirids for the Fatimids and then for the Abbasids. Later the Almohad caliphate, and the Ottoman pashas, deys and beys.
caliphate.dates: 647 raid (tribute, no occupation); 670–800 Umayyad/Abbasid direct (Carthage 698; Kharijite seizure of Kairouan 745/758 aside); 800–909 Aghlabid; 909–973 Fatimid direct; 973–c.1048 Zirid for the Fatimids, then for the Abbasids to 1148/1160; 1159/60–1229 Almohad; 1574–1881 Ottoman

units.notes: The 647 battle of Sufetula (Sbeitla, Kassérine) was a Rashidun raid bought off with tribute, not a conquest. Lasting rule began with Kairouan in 670. The Norman Kingdom of Africa held Mahdia and some coastal towns (1148–1160) and Spain held Tunis 1535–1574, so the coast had breaks. Under the Husainids Ottoman suzerainty became largely formal.
units.uncertain: The exact dates of Norman and Spanish coastal enclaves within each province were not mapped. The Zirid switch to the Abbasids is given as 1041–1051 in the opened source.

summary: Cyrenaica (Barqa) and Tripoli were conquered by Amr ibn al-As under the Rashidun caliph Umar in 642–643. Cyrenaica then followed Egypt (Umayyad, Abbasid, Fatimid, Ayyubid, Mamluk) and Tripolitania followed Ifriqiya (Aghlabid, Fatimid, Zirid, Almohad, Hafsid). The Ottomans held Tripoli from 1551 and Benghazi from 1578, directly or through the Karamanlis (1711–1835). The Fezzan was raided in 642 and 666–67 and then ruled by local Muslim dynasties (Ibadi Banu Khattab, Kanem, Awlad Muhammad); the Awlad Muhammad were tributary to the Ottomans, who ruled directly from 1842. Kufra was never really under any caliph; the Sanusiyya made it their centre from 1895.

units.label: Tripolitania coast (Ṭarābulus al-Gharb)

caliphate.who: Rashidun conquest, Umayyad and Abbasid governors, Aghlabids for the Abbasids, the Fatimids, Zirids, the Almohads, and the Ottomans (directly, via the Karamanlis, then directly again)
caliphate.dates: 643 Rashidun (Tripoli taken); Umayyad/Abbasid to 800 (Ibadi Abu al-Khattab held Tripoli 757–761); Aghlabid 800–909 (Tripolitania ceded to the Rustamids for a time after 812); Fatimid 909–973; Zirid from 978; Almohad c. 1160; Ottoman 1551–1911 (Karamanli 1711–1835)

units.notes: Tripoli fell to Amr ibn al-As after about a month's siege in 643, making the coast one of the earliest caliph-ruled parts of the Maghreb. Rule was interrupted by Ibadi revolts, the Normans (Tripoli taken in 1146, not checked here), Spain (1510–1530) and the Knights of St John (1530–1551). The Karamanlis were hereditary rulers under nominal Ottoman suzerainty.
units.uncertain: The Norman occupation of Tripoli (1146–1158) was not confirmed in an opened page. Surt (the Sirte gulf) was thinly settled and ruled mainly as a route.

units.label: Fezzan and the Jufra oases (Fazzān, Zawīla, Waddān)

caliphate.who: First, Rashidun and Umayyad expeditions (Waddan tribute 642; Uqba's military post 666–67). Then Ottoman suzerainty over the local Awlad Muhammad sultans with a garrison at Murzuq, and direct Ottoman rule from 1842.
caliphate.dates: 642 tribute (Waddan); 666–67 Uqba's conquest/raid; Ottoman from 1574/1580s (tributary sultans + garrison); direct Ottoman 1842–1912

units.notes: Early Muslim armies raided the Fezzan and Waddan and took tribute, and Uqba left a military post at Waddan. For about 900 years after that, though, the Fezzan was ruled by local or Saharan Muslim dynasties that recognised no caliph (Ibadi Banu Khattab, Kanem). From the 1570s–80s the Awlad Muhammad gave allegiance to the Ottoman sultan, with a garrison, and direct Ottoman rule came only in 1842. The Rustamid imamate's influence reached Zawila (9th c.).
units.uncertain: It is unclear whether Uqba's 666 campaign or any Abbasid-era governor left lasting administration. The Ottoman tribute amounts, garrison continuity and the exact start of Awlad Muhammad rule are disputed.

units.notes: Kufra was Tebu country until the Zuwayya Arabs took it in 1808. The Sanusiyya ran it as a religious-political authority, but it was not a formal state with a caliph.
units.uncertain: Whether the Sanusiyya formally acknowledged the Ottoman sultan-caliph is not settled in the sources I opened, which stress tension and autonomy. It is debatable whether the order counts as an 'Islamic state'.

summary: No caliph ever administered Mauritania. It was ruled instead by Muslim powers that did not formally recognise a caliph. In the north, the Almoravid movement rose among the Sanhaja in the 1040s–1050s, with Azougui in the Adrar as its first capital; Abu Bakr ibn Umar ruled the Saharan wing until he died in Tagant in 1087. The south-east was in Ghana's and then Mali's sphere (Walata a Mali garrison town). The Senegal valley had Muslim Takrur (from c. 1035) and the Futa Toro Imamate (1776). From the 17th century the Hassaniya emirates (Trarza, Brakna, Adrar, Tagant) ruled until French protectorates (1902–1912).

units.notes: Azougui was the first Almoravid capital and fortress, and Abu Bakr ibn Umar made it his base after 1072. He died in Tagant in 1087, after which the Saharan confederation split among his and his brother's descendants. Later the Hassaniya emirates governed these plateaus until the French conquest of the Adrar (1908–1912).
units.uncertain: I did not confirm whether the Saharan Almoravids named the Abbasid caliph in the khutba or on coins. If they did, the category would rise to caliphate_ruled (nominal). The Emirate of Tagant's dates come from general knowledge, not an opened page; the Tagant page I opened only says Adrar migrants settled there in the mid-17th c.

units.label: The Hodh and Assaba (Awdaghust, Walāta, Kumbi Saleh)

islamic_states.name: Mali Empire (garrisons at Oualata and Koumbi)

units.notes: Awdaghust (Tegdaoust, Hodh el Gharbi) was a Ghana-aligned trading town until the Almoravids stormed it in 1054–55. Whether they then conquered Ghana (Koumbi Saleh, Hodh ech Chargui) is disputed. Mali held Walata and Koumbi with garrisons until losing Walata to the Tuareg (1430s). Songhai under Askia Muhammad took Walata briefly and settled for tribute.
units.uncertain: Askia Muhammad bore the title khalifa after his hajj (1496–98), but the opened source does not say who conferred it (an Abbasid shadow caliph in Cairo or the Sharif of Mecca), so I did not count it as caliph rule. Assaba's own history was not checked.
